commenti.body:
I honestly think Preston Sturges  biggest strength is in part his biggest flaw. 

That is to say his ability to to kind of wade into the earlier genres of screwball comedy and silent era-ish slapstick is in part of why I think he's not really thought of as being more forward thinking.

With someone like Welles or Huston, the ability to craft stories that were more down to earth and gritty in contrast with earlier cinema works kind of cemented them as a sort of street level auteur.

But I think that Sturges' movies are more designed to kind of feel like echoes of a better year, a sort of fanfare to the tongue in cheek in farce.. Sullivan's Travels being an odd ode to escapist cinema as it pulls away from that approach. 

I do think that Preston Sturges is kind of like George Cukor in that 50 years ago, he'd probably be a household name with contemporary film studies.

But I do believe that the splintering of the discipline into auteur appreciation and arguably into didactic response has made it so     that watching movies as either an extension of competent studio practice or personal style is a bit on the taboo side.  

I think films are now more valued for what they preport to argue than for their abilities to function as dramatic or entertaining material.  

The propaganization of storytelling is something that I think that movies is political artforms has been there kind of since the beginning ( hard to not believe a Trip to the Moon is a colonist fantasy)  but I do think that what is happening is topics kind of chipping away at art.  

So going back to Preston Sturges, I think that the greatest barrier is the pre-1970s era. Father time is brutal.

>I think films are now more valued for what they preport to argue than for their abilities to function as dramatic or entertaining material.

It's interesting you say that because *Sullivan's Travels* is, among everything else, a critique of just that mindset.

* No disagreement here. I think the idea of Sullivan wanting to make a weighty, heavy-handed film in part because of his own insulation and becoming more appreciative of ecapist fair as he's wrung through the wringer is a very apt.

I was talking more about how I think the critical mindset of film response is going, though I do think with good films, they can stand alone from the ideological subtext.

A example for me would be Citizen Kane and it's critique of the media moguls of the day ( Hearst and Pulitzer namely) that's something that maybe an audience member would understand or not, but the more immediate kind of Charles Dickens like tale of a man who pushes everyone he cares about away is timeless.

When I was referencing my critique of film discourse, I was thinking more in that kind of Academic school of thought.  

I do think that the college film appreciation kind of went on the wrong fork of the train tracks. I believe it's a case of wanting media to reflect contemporary thought processes, which inevitably makes old films harder to justify, and new films serving as a sort of echo chamber. 

I mean I'll use a lazy analogy but... video games. 

It's not like you're going to have your controller, have the character move around, then wait for a a non player character say something that you disagree with.. and then decide if the game is good or bad based on what the NPC said. 

I think by reducing appreciation to agreement, one devalues both.

I love Sturges and think he's underrated, but his greatest strength was certainly his writing and not his visual style.

If your looking for influence in contemporary films Martin McDonagh (*The Banshees of Inisherin*) is one example. I haven't even seen the movie, but after watching the trailer I specifically Googled if he was a fan or not.

Honestly I think the biggest reason he's not as well known is that his films are all a bit "off". He doesn't mind making chaotic plot decisions in the middle (Sullivan's Travels) or end of the film (Palm Beach Story) and his stories don't have traditional feel good endings (even if they're technically happy endings.)

*Unfaithfully Yours* is usually considered outside Sturges' string of hits. This was in part because of the dark tones which were confused in the marketing -- and that, in turn, was in part because of a tragic scandal involving Rex Harrison in a scenario uncomfortably close to the events depicted in the film.

A film I think deserves to climb into the Great Hollywood Canon is *Remember the Night*. The screenplay is by Sturges and juxtaposes small-town Americana against Big City cynicism to paint a deftly poignant Christmas romance. It isn't signature Sturges screwball and would drift into schmaltzville were it not for a neat writing and nuanced acting by one of the great pairings from the studio era, Fred MacMurray & Barbara Stanwyck.

Preston Sturges is one of the greats. Sullivan’s Travels is one of my favorites, I’d easily put it somewhere in my top 20. 

His movies definitely require some familiarity with the other movies of the time to really “get”. When I saw The Lady Eve some of it went over my head a little bit. I couldn’t get over the fact that Henry Fonda’s character would fall for the same girl twice without realizing it’s the same girl. That’s the whole point of course, but nowadays movies are so concerned with believability that it maybe doesn’t resonate with people as much. His movies always have these way out there premises that are a bit hard to submit yourself to. But once you do you’ll be rewarded thoroughly.

>Preston Sturges is one of the greats.

Any thoughts as to why many cinephiles don't seem to take him seriously? Is part of it what you cite, his relative lack of interest in a strict verisimilitude?

My mind goes to two filmmakers I mention in the original post, Quentin Tarantino and Wes Anderson. Would anyone describe either's films as realistic, as 'slices of life'? In both cases, a lot of what people like about these filmmakers is precisely that they offer a stylized, heightened version of reality.

Good catch. McDonagh has [listed](https://www.metro.us/three-billboards-outside-ebbing-missouri-writer-and-director-martinmcdonagh-reveals-his-writing-habits/) Preston Sturges as one of his favorite filmmakers, along with Sam Peckinpah and Powell & Pressburger.
The Palm Beach Story has one of the funniest endings I’ve ever seen lol

He is one of the great pioneers of film comedy in the sound era. He has that scintillating fast-paced dialogue that became a staple of screwball comedy. Unfaithfully Yours is definitely my favorite. I also like Sullivan's Travels, which was screened in my film class and was my introduction to his work. The Lady Eve and some of the others are uneven, I think, but have some great moments.

I think Preston Sturges is fairly placed in the pantheon of filmmaking; four of his movies are placed on the 'They Shoot Pictures Don't They' list. 

Besides the point I made in my first comment I think it also has to with him primarily being a great writer and just a good director. Unfortunately the level of dialogue in movies has been going down for the past half a century (in my humblest opinion). Nowadays attention is mostly given to the directors that have a distinct visual flair (for example most critics now prefer Buster Keaton to Charlie Chaplin), which Preston Sturges didn't have.

>EDIT: To your point about filmmakers today. Preston Sturges made it a point to intentionally thwart narrative conventions, sometimes a bit unsatisfyingly. 

Do you mean something like *The Palm Beach* story, a romantic comedy which ends with an intentionally absurd joke about the contrivances of romantic comedy endings?
I recently watched it (part of Criterion's 'Barbara Stanwyck Christmas' double feature) and quite enjoyed it.

His autobiography is not only a great account of his rise to success and fall from those heights, but it is a hilarious, engaging, rollercoaster ride through the aristocratic life that led him around the world as a child with his globetrotting mother.

Sturges is one of my favorite filmmakers. I love reading his screenplays and rewatching his films, all of which makes you laugh and get better and better with each viewing. Through the years I have found he is the most lasting comedic styling for modern audiences. Whenever I get someone to give him a chance, they are always surprised that these forties movies humor is so fresh and funny. His influence is clear in all the film makers you mentioned, and many who don't even know of him. He was a pioneer.

My personal favorites are Hail the Conquering Hero and Christmas in July. William Demarest is always the greatest gift in these films. What a classic character actor. Don't sleep on Sturges!
Would you agree that he's underrated?

I would say, since his time, he has been considered one of the most innovative, time tested, auteur geniuses (as you cited in those opinions). I do not know if it is just his star that is waning in the modern school or every one of my favorite film makers. You could say he is underrated at the moment, but time will eventually place him at the top where he has been and always belongs.

Preston sturges is very well known. Even his lesser movies are well known. I consider unfaithfully yours, miracle at morgan creek, and Christmas in july to be lesser movies. Unfaithfully yours started out well with the ideal plans set out only to have the implementation fail pathetically.  While this narrative worked in gambit, UY became predictable with the only question is how many wicker chairs he owned. The weak second act dictated the weak ending.

christmas in july is a shocker. The director who gave us some cynical movies, gave us this movie where he shows the common man can be filled by consumeris. Wow!

my favorite sturges is hail the conquering hero. It  is the most unpredictable of his scripts.
Yes. Out of left field in the best possible way, and a hilarious spoof of the cliched romcom ending.

>Besides the point I made in my first comment I think it also has to with him primarily being a great writer and just a good director.

I think there's an argument to be made for Sturges as a very good if not great director of actors: who else got better performances from Joel McCrea, for instance? Or Veronica Lake? Or brought out the comedic side (and comedic timing) of the otherwise earnest, dramatic Henry Fonda? And of course he's known for his 'stock company' of character actors who always give memorably vivid performances in his films.
